results.result: The study analyzed 407 neonates (355 term-born, 52 preterm-born) from the dHCP dataset, with mean GA of 39.93±1.26 weeks and PT of 1.21±1.25 weeks. GA and PT were not significantly correlated (r=-0.08, p>0.1), allowing independent assessment of prenatal and postnatal influences.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C6-C7, and C87-C90 provide comprehensive sample characterization with appropriate exclusion criteria, demographic details, and statistical validation of GA-PT independence. The large sample size (n=407) and rigorous quality control strengthen the study design.

results.result: CT and CM in ventral cortex significantly increased with PMA (r=0.40-0.49, p<10⁻⁹), with spatial gradients showing stronger correlations in posterior versus anterior regions (r=-0.8 and -0.83, p<0.001) and medial versus lateral regions (r=0.7 and 0.91, p<0.001).
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C5 demonstrate clear developmental trajectories with strong statistical support and organized spatial patterns. The correlation coefficients and p-values indicate robust effects, though the negative correlation values in C4 appear inconsistent with the stated 'higher correlation' interpretation.

results.result: GA strongly influenced CM (r=0.53-0.51, p<10⁻⁹ for whole ventral cortex; significant in all 68 ROIs) but weakly influenced CT (r=0.16-0.14, p<0.05; significant in only 23/68 ROIs). Conversely, PT strongly influenced CT (r=0.53-0.51, p<10⁻⁹; significant in 61/68 ROIs) but not CM (r=0.02-0.01, p>0.6). Linear mixed-effect models confirmed GA had significantly stronger effects on CM than PT (p<0.05), with no differential effects on CT (p>0.6).
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C13 provide converging evidence from whole-brain and regional analyses with appropriate statistical corrections (FDR) and mixed-effect modeling. The dissociation between GA effects on CM versus PT effects on CT is well-documented, though the lack of differential effects on CT (C13) appears somewhat inconsistent with the strong PT-CT correlations reported.

results.result: In V1 and VOTC specifically, CT development was modulated by both PT (r=0.26-0.52, p<10⁻⁶) and GA (r=0.18-0.29, p<10⁻³), while CM development was influenced by GA (r=0.43-0.51, p<10⁻⁶) but not PT (r=0.02-0.09, p>0.05). Mixed-effect models showed no differential GA versus PT influence on CT (p>0.3), but CM showed significantly different impacts in V1 (p<0.01) and marginal significance in VOTC (p<0.09).
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C16 provide region-specific validation of the whole-brain patterns with appropriate statistical testing. The exception for left VOTC CT (r=0.01) and left V1 CM (r=0.12, p=0.03) are appropriately noted, though these exceptions somewhat weaken the overall pattern.

results.result: In infants scanned within the first day after birth (n=73), homotopic connections were significant in all ventral cortex ROIs (mean r=0.13-0.43, t>12.87, p<10⁻⁹) and significantly higher than adjacent (0.29±0.12 vs 0.19±0.10, z=16.32, p<10⁻⁹) and distal connections (0.04±0.06, z=16.32, p<10⁻⁹). Community structure analysis identified three functional clusters (lateral, medial, and anterior-lateral temporal), suggesting proto-organization of ventral visual cortex exists at birth before higher-level visual experience.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C21 demonstrate innate functional organization with appropriate statistical testing and multiple analytical approaches (homotopic correlations, community structure analysis). The use of infants scanned within 1 day of birth effectively controls for postnatal experience, though the sample size (n=73) is relatively small for network analyses.

results.result: Homotopic connections increased with PMA in V1 and lateral-anterior regions (16/34 regions, r=0.12-0.27, FDR q<0.05). GA correlated with homotopic connections in anterior temporal cortex (14/34 patches, r=0.12-0.28, FDR q<0.05), while PT correlated with connections in V1, fusiform, and anterior temporal areas (6/34 patches, r=0.14-0.22, FDR q<0.05). Network measures (global efficiency and mean cluster coefficient) increased with PMA (r=0.25-0.27, p<0.001) and correlated with both GA (r=0.11-0.13, p<0.05) and PT (r=0.22-0.25, p<0.001).
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C26 demonstrate developmental changes in functional connectivity with appropriate multiple comparison corrections. The regional specificity of GA versus PT effects is well-documented, though the relatively modest correlation coefficients suggest these effects are moderate in magnitude.

results.result: Homotopic V1 connections (r=0.43±0.25) were significantly stronger than homotopic VOTC connections (r=0.38±0.22, t=4.29, p<10⁻⁴), both of which exceeded ipsilateral V1-VOTC connections (r=0.16±0.19, t=15.74 and 13.49, p<10⁻⁹). Homotopic connections in V1 and VOTC increased with PMA (r=0.16-0.18, p<0.01) and were modulated by PT (r=-0.20 and -0.11, p<0.05) but not GA (r=-0.01 and 0.09, p>0.05). Ipsilateral V1-VOTC connections decreased with PMA (r=-0.23, p<10⁻⁴) and correlated with both PT and GA (r=-0.19 and -0.13, p<0.05).
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C32 show internally inconsistent patterns: homotopic connections reportedly increase with PMA (C29) but are negatively correlated with PT (C31, r=-0.20 and -0.11). Since PMA increases with PT, these opposing signs are contradictory. This inconsistency undermines confidence in the reported PT effects on functional connectivity.

results.result: Mediation analysis revealed PT had a significant direct effect on bilateral V1 homotopic connections not mediated by CT or CM, while GA's effect on these connections was indirect, mediated through CM rather than direct.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C34 report mediation analyses but provide insufficient methodological detail (no effect sizes, confidence intervals, or specific p-values for indirect effects). The contradictory correlation patterns noted in the previous result (C31 showing negative PT correlations) further complicate interpretation of these mediation effects.

results.result: Comparing matched term-born (n=52) and preterm-born infants (n=52) at equivalent PMA (40.92±1.87 vs 40.90±1.91 weeks), term-born infants had higher GA (39.96±1.40 vs 31.98±3.32 weeks, t=14.04, p<10⁻⁹) but lower PT (0.96±1.13 vs 8.91±4.42 weeks, t=-13.86, p<10⁻⁹). Term-born infants showed lower mean CT (1.39±0.05 vs 1.35±0.05, t=-3.16, p<0.01) in 10/68 ROIs including V1 (t=-2.55, p<0.02) but not VOTC. Term-born infants showed higher mean CM (1.22±0.10 vs 1.09±0.08, t=7.11, p<10⁻⁹) in all 68 ROIs including V1 and VOTC (t=6.65 and 7.54, p<10⁻⁸).
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C41 provide well-controlled comparison between term and preterm infants with matched PMA, appropriate sample sizes, and strong statistical support. The findings validate the differential effects of GA on CM and PT on CT observed in the correlational analyses, though confounding environmental factors (NICU exposure) are acknowledged as limitations.

results.result: Term-born infants showed higher global efficiency and mean cluster coefficient than preterm-born infants (t=2.22 and 2.43, p<0.05), suggesting higher efficiency of information transmission and cortical differentiation. Preterm-born infants showed lower arealization in VOTC (t=3.75, p<0.001) but not V1 (t=1.60, p>0.1), suggesting GA influences bilateral visual cortex connections.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C44 provide statistical support for functional network differences between groups, though the effect sizes are modest (t=2.22-2.43). Claim C45 is an inference from group differences rather than direct evidence of GA effects. The interpretation in C43 about 'higher efficiency' is reasonable but somewhat speculative.

results.result: The study concludes that human visual cortex development does not strictly follow the two-stage hypothesis (experience-independent followed by experience-dependent), as cortical properties are modulated by postnatal environment within the first month of life. Early cortical development represents a mixed outcome of endogenous and experience-dependent processes in both structure and function, with postnatal experience selectively modifying endogenous development.
results.evaluation: Claims C46, C81-C82 represent the main conclusions synthesizing the empirical findings. The evidence for PT effects on CT and functional connectivity supports these conclusions, though the contradictory correlation patterns (C31) and acknowledged confounds (NICU environment, C83-C84) introduce some uncertainty about the specificity of 'postnatal experience' versus other factors.

results.result: CT relates to synaptogenesis and synaptic pruning shaped by innate and postnatal factors. Previous literature showed CT increases to maximum during first 2 years then thins, mirroring synaptic trajectories, with similar patterns in blind and sighted subjects suggesting visual experience is not necessary. The current study suggests postnatal environment could accelerate cortical thickening even if not necessary.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C66 appropriately contextualize findings within established neurodevelopmental literature with proper citations. The interpretation that PT 'accelerates' rather than is 'necessary' for CT development is reasonable given the data, though direct comparison with blind infants would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: T1w/T2w-based CM serves as a surrogate marker of myelination related to cognitive performance and likely reflects myelinated fiber increases. While previous studies showed experience-dependent CM development in older children (5-12 years), the current study found CM correlated with GA but not PT in neonates, suggesting early myelination is primarily determined by endogenic growth in utero. The posterior-to-anterior CM spatial pattern observed agrees with previous findings at 6 months and occurs as early as the neonatal period.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C73 appropriately describe the CM measure with citations and contextualize findings within developmental literature. The conclusion that early myelination is 'primarily' endogenic is well-supported by the strong GA correlations and absent PT correlations, though potential confounds from partial volume effects (C85-C86) are acknowledged.

results.result: Two distinct visual clusters along the medial-lateral axis captured the central-peripheral organization of ventral visual system. The lateral area becomes face-selective while medial area specializes in scene/building processing later in life, suggesting an innate scaffold is established at birth for subsequent experience-dependent modification.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C76 appropriately interpret the functional clustering results in the context of known visual system organization with proper citations. The inference about an 'innate scaffold' is reasonable given the presence of organized connectivity at birth (within 1 day), though longitudinal data would strengthen causal claims about subsequent modification.

results.result: Homotopic connections in human neonates were lower than in macaque neonates, potentially due to higher motion, less fMRI data, coarser parcellation, and species developmental differences. Decreased V1-VOTC connections with PMA might reflect functional differentiation between adjacent regions. Increased homotopic connections could be direct or indirect (e.g., mediated by thalamus).
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C80 appropriately acknowledge methodological limitations and alternative interpretations. The speculation about mechanisms (C78, C80) is reasonable and appropriately qualified. The comparison to macaque data (C77) provides useful cross-species context, though direct quantitative comparison is limited by methodological differences.

results.result: The study acknowledges limitations including uncontrolled environmental differences between preterm (potentially NICU) and term-born infants, inability to separate combined GA and PT effects in group comparisons, and potential partial-volume effects on CM measurements due to changing cortical thickness during development.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C86 appropriately acknowledge important limitations that affect interpretation of the preterm versus term comparisons and CM measurements. These limitations are significant and appropriately disclosed, though they somewhat undermine the strength of conclusions about specific 'postnatal experience' effects versus other confounding factors.

results.result: The manuscript reviews prior literature establishing the two-stage developmental framework (experience-independent then experience-dependent), recent evidence for early experience effects in animals, methodological challenges in infant neuroimaging, the dHCP project, and limitations of previous human infant studies (small samples, inability to control for postnatal experience). The rationale for using GA-PT differences as a proxy for postnatal experience variation is established.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C61 appropriately review relevant literature with proper citations and establish the study rationale. The identification of gaps in previous research (small samples, confounded postnatal experience) is accurate and justifies the current study design, though the proxy measure (PT) has acknowledged limitations regarding specificity to visual experience.

results.result: The ventral cortex was parcellated into 34 ROIs per hemisphere using the HCP-MMP atlas, including V1, V2, VOTC (15 ROIs including parahippocampus, middle fusiform, lateral occipital cortex), and anterior temporal cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C92 clearly describe the anatomical parcellation scheme with appropriate citations. The use of adult atlas registered to neonatal template is acknowledged as a limitation elsewhere, with validation showing reasonable registration quality (dice coefficient 0.80-0.83 for V1).

results.result: The study used a large dataset of 407 neonates from the dHCP project, with 355 term-born infants. The sample showed no significant correlation between GA and PT (r = -0.08, p>0.1), allowing separation of prenatal and postnatal developmental factors.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praised the use of the large dHCP dataset, stating it 'is impressive and strengthens the claims made in the paper.' The sample characteristics and lack of GA-PT correlation are not questioned, supporting the study's ability to separate developmental factors.

results.result: CT and CM of ventral cortex significantly increased with PMA (r = 0.40-0.49, p<10^-9), with spatial gradients showing higher correlations in posterior than anterior regions and medial than lateral parts.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raised concerns about the use of PMA in analyses, with all three reviewers requesting clarification and simplification of terminology. Reviewer 1 stated 'it's difficult to see the relationship of the GA on CT and CM separately' when PMA is used, suggesting the analysis should focus on GA and PT separately rather than PMA.

results.result: GA was significantly related to CM across all 68 ROIs but to CT in only 23 ROIs, while PT was significantly correlated with CT in 61 ROIs but showed minimal correlation with CM. Linear mixed-effect models showed GA had significantly stronger effect on CM than PT (p<0.05).
results.evaluation: While reviewers did not directly challenge these findings, they expressed confusion about the analyses and requested clarification. Reviewer 1 noted confusion about terminology and suggested moving supplementary figures showing GA and PT effects to main figures. Reviewers 1 and 3 requested a summary table of which measures were modulated by GA versus PT, suggesting the current presentation is unclear.

results.result: In V1 and VOTC specifically, CT development was modulated by both PT and GA, while CM development was significantly influenced by GA but not PT, with linear mixed-effect models showing significantly different impacts in V1 (p<0.01).
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these regional findings. Reviewer 1 specifically praised supplementary figures showing these effects (4c and 4f) and suggested they 'make your point on the postnatal age and GA influence on CT and CM really clear,' indicating acceptance of these differential effects.

results.result: Homotopic connections in ventral cortex were significant in infants scanned within the first day after birth (mean r = 0.13-0.43, p<10^-9), significantly higher than adjacent and distal connections, suggesting proto-organization of ventral visual cortex exists at birth.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raised important concerns about the homotopy analysis, noting that 'comparing 34 homotopic pairs with the hundreds of non-homotopic pairs' is problematic and suggested an alternative test. Reviewer 1 requested clarification about what 'non-homotopic' means and how r=0.09 could be significant. These methodological concerns cast uncertainty on the conclusions about proto-organization.

results.result: Homotopic connections and network measures (global efficiency, mean cluster coefficient) showed developmental increases with PMA, with differential effects of GA and PT across regions.
results.evaluation: Similar to other PMA-based analyses, reviewers requested clarification and simplification of terminology. The specific findings about regional differences in GA versus PT effects are not directly challenged, but the overall analytical approach using PMA is questioned by all reviewers.

results.result: V1 and VOTC showed different patterns of homotopic connectivity development, with V1 showing higher homotopic correlation than VOTC. Homotopic connections increased with PMA while ipsilateral V1-VOTC connections decreased, with PT but not GA modulating homotopic correlations.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not directly challenge these specific findings, but Reviewer 1 requested clarification about negative connectivity and what it would imply. The broader concerns about functional connectivity analyses and terminology apply to these claims as well.

results.result: Mediation analysis showed PT had a significant direct effect on homotopic V1 connections not mediated by CT or CM, while GA's effect was indirect through CM.
results.evaluation: Reviewers 1 and 3 expressed confusion about the section comparing structural and functional properties, with Reviewer 3 stating they 'were expecting the authors to more formally compare structural and functional development' and suggesting regression analyses with functional connectivity and structural metrics. The current mediation analysis may not fully address what reviewers expected.

results.result: Term-born infants showed lower CT but higher CM than preterm-born infants at equivalent PMA, with higher network efficiency and greater arealization in VOTC, suggesting GA influences bilateral visual cortex connections.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 noted confusion about statements regarding CT differences, pointing out contradictory statements about whether term-born infants had higher or lower CT in V1. Reviewer 3 raised an important concern about partial-volume effects, noting that 'a thinner cortex, given constant-sized voxels, is more likely to be biased by white matter signal,' which could confound the myelin differences observed between groups.

results.result: The study concludes that human visual cortex development does not strictly follow the two-stage hypothesis, as postnatal experience selectively modifies endogenous development even within the first month of life, with early myelination primarily determined by endogenic growth in utero while cortical thickness is accelerated by postnatal environment.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 questioned whether the term 'postnatal experience' is appropriate, suggesting the authors 'tone it down to postnatal time, as we don't have any behavioral measure of visual experience per se.' This challenges the interpretation that the findings reflect 'experience' rather than simply time. The broader conclusions about the two-stage hypothesis are not directly challenged but depend on the validity of the underlying analyses.

results.result: The study used the adult HCP-MMP atlas to parcellate ventral cortex into 34 ROIs per hemisphere, including V1, VOTC (15 ROIs), and anterior temporal cortex.
results.evaluation: Reviewers 1 and 3 requested a 'sanity check' of how well the adult Glasser atlas aligns on neonatal brains at different ages, with Reviewer 1 suggesting comparing alignment at 37 weeks versus 42 weeks and running statistics on cortical-based alignments. Reviewer 2 also suggested considering the Wang et al. (2015) atlas as an alternative. The lack of validation raises uncertainty about the appropriateness of using adult parcellations.

results.result: The authors acknowledge limitations including different environments for preterm infants (e.g., NICU), inability to fully separate GA and PT effects in group comparisons, and potential partial-volume effects on CM measurements.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly raised these concerns, with Reviewer 3 noting the partial-volume issue and Reviewer 2 suggesting alternative analyses to better control for confounds. The authors' acknowledgment of these limitations is appropriate, though reviewers suggest additional analyses or controls are needed.

results.result: The posterior-to-anterior spatial pattern of CM and medial-lateral clustering observed in neonates matches patterns seen in older infants, suggesting an innate scaffold is established at birth for subsequent experience-dependent modification.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 noted that 'results of more myelination in the V1 than higher-order areas are consistent with the hierarchical findings of a prior paper' (Natu et al., 2021) and found it 'interesting to see is that neural scaffolding starts to develop early on during prenatal life,' indicating acceptance of these findings about early organization.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on sample characterization (C1, C2, C6, C7, C87-C90). Both evaluations find the large dHCP dataset and lack of GA-PT correlation strengthen the study design. OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, peer reviewers explicitly praised these aspects.

Disagreement on developmental trajectories (C3-C5). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED despite noting inconsistencies in correlation interpretation. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, raising concerns about PMA usage and requesting clarification on separating GA and PT effects.

Partial disagreement on whole-brain analyses (C8-C13). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED with strong statistical evidence. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, expressing confusion about analyses and requesting clarification, summary tables, and moving supplementary figures to main text.

Agreement on region-specific findings (C14-C16). Both evaluations find these results supported. OpenEval notes appropriate statistical testing with some exceptions. Peer reviewers praised supplementary figures showing these effects as making the point clear.

Disagreement on innate functional organization (C17-C21). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED despite small sample size. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, raising methodological concerns about homotopy analysis comparing 34 homotopic pairs with hundreds of non-homotopic pairs.

Disagreement on functional connectivity development (C22-C26). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED with appropriate corrections. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, requesting clarification and simplification of PMA-based terminology across all reviewers.

Both rate UNCERTAIN on homotopic connectivity patterns (C27-C32). OpenEval identifies internal inconsistencies between PMA and PT correlations. Peer reviewers request clarification about negative connectivity but do not directly challenge the specific findings.

Both rate UNCERTAIN on mediation analyses (C33-C34). OpenEval cites insufficient methodological detail and contradictory patterns. Peer reviewers express confusion about structural-functional comparisons and suggest more formal regression analyses.

Disagreement on term vs preterm comparisons (C35-C41). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED with strong statistical support despite acknowledged confounds. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, noting contradictory statements about CT differences and raising concerns about partial-volume effects confounding myelin differences.

Partial overlap on group differences (C42-C45). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED for functional network differences with modest effect sizes. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN for the broader term vs preterm comparison, citing contradictions and partial-volume concerns.

Disagreement on main conclusions (C46, C81-C82). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED while noting contradictory patterns and confounds introduce uncertainty. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, questioning whether 'postnatal experience' is appropriate versus 'postnatal time' given lack of behavioral measures.

Partial overlap on contextual interpretation (C62-C66). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED for contextualization within literature. Peer reviewers question the 'postnatal experience' terminology (C66), suggesting it should be toned down to 'postnatal time.'

Agreement on CM measure and early myelination (C67-C73). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED for hierarchical organization and endogenic myelination. Peer reviewers also find hierarchical V1 myelination consistent with prior work and accept early neural scaffolding development.

Agreement on functional clustering interpretation (C74-C76). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED for innate scaffold interpretation with appropriate citations. Peer reviewers find it interesting that neural scaffolding develops early during prenatal life, indicating acceptance.
OpenEval rates SUPPORTED for methodological limitations and alternative interpretations (C77-C80). No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific limitation acknowledgments.

Agreement on limitations (C83-C86). Both evaluations rate SUPPORTED for acknowledging confounds from NICU environment and partial-volume effects. Peer reviewers explicitly raised these concerns and find the acknowledgment appropriate, though suggest additional analyses.
